sources.title: Moche Portrait Vessels
sources.author: Moche Ceramicists
sources.excerpt: Each face is unique - scars, wrinkles, expressions captured in clay with photographic precision.
sources.longExcerpt: The Moche of Peru's north coast created portrait vessels unlike anything in the ancient world. Not idealized gods or generic humans, but individuals - this man's broken nose, that woman's distinctive cheekbones, an elder's wrinkled smile. Some show the same person at different ages. Were they rulers? Ancestors? The vessels held chicha beer for ceremonies where the dead drank with the living. Each portrait preserves a soul, a name we'll never know, a life lived fifteen centuries ago.

sources.title: Nazca Geoglyph Records
sources.author: Nazca culture
sources.excerpt: The great lines stretch across the desert floor, visible only from the mountains above. They form the shapes of animals, plants, and geometric patterns, created for the gods to see from the sky.
sources.longExcerpt: The great lines stretch across the desert floor, visible only from the mountains above. They form the shapes of animals, plants, and geometric patterns, created for the gods to see from the sky. These massive geoglyphs in Peru's Nazca Desert, created between 200-700 CE, include images of hummingbirds, spiders, monkeys, and other figures that can only be fully appreciated from an aerial perspective.

sources.title: Gate of the Sun Inscriptions
sources.author: Tiwanaku priests
sources.excerpt: The great gateway stands beneath the central figure of the Staff God, surrounded by running attendants who carry staffs and wear elaborate headdresses. This marks the calendar of our ceremonies and the movements of the sun.
sources.longExcerpt: The great gateway stands beneath the central figure of the Staff God, surrounded by running attendants who carry staffs and wear elaborate headdresses. This marks the calendar of our ceremonies and the movements of the sun. The Gate of the Sun at Tiwanaku, Bolivia, represents one of the most important religious and astronomical monuments in pre-Columbian South America, dating to around 800 CE.

citation.modernSource: Academia Nacional de Ciencias de Bolivia, 1945
